title: Databases: Storing Your Data for Good

intro.text: Everything your app has saved so far lives in the browser — refresh the page on another device and it's gone. This chapter fixes that. You'll learn what a database is and why every real service has one, spin up a free cloud database with Supabase, learn how tables, primary keys, and foreign keys actually work, and then direct the AI to wire the Ohana Link app so every folder and link is stored permanently — verifying each step in the Supabase dashboard yourself. You'll finish with a debugging playbook, so when errors inevitably show up you can diagnose them instead of just forwarding them.

lessons.title: Introducing Databases
lessons.objective: Understand what a database is, why it's needed, and how it operates — well enough to spot when a setup is missing its always-on machine or its backend bodyguard.

intro.text: Starting with this chapter we tackle the database — the place where data is kept permanently. In this first lesson we'll look at what a database is, why we need one, and how it works behind the scenes. You won't build any of this by hand, but you can't judge work you can't name — so this vocabulary is your foundation.

blocks.text: A database is a computer program built to manage large amounts of data efficiently. It does far more than just store things:
It stores complex data by breaking it into a clean structure
It connects related pieces of data to each other
It finds the data you need fast

These days it's hard to find a program that doesn't use a database — it's a core building block of almost every service. Starting this chapter, our Ohana Link project grows up too: it will begin saving its data in a database.
“Strictly speaking, the ‘database’ is the collection of data, and the program that manages it is called a DBMS — but in everyday use, people call the whole thing a database.”
blocks.title: Another way to think about it

steps.title: What it takes to run a database

blocks.text: A database is, in the end, a computer program. It can't float in mid-air — for the program to run, there has to be a computer running it.

But an ordinary PC won't cut it. Users hit your service at 3 a.m. and on weekends, so the database has to be up at those hours too. In other words, you need a computer that is turned on 24/7 and never switched off.
So can users just connect straight to that database and pull their data out themselves?

This is where things break down. A database was never designed to take requests directly from end users. Its communication features are minimal, and leaving it open to anyone is a security incident waiting to happen — the moment one password leaks, the entire dataset can be stolen.

That's why a go-between server always sits next to the database. It receives user requests on the database's behalf, checks permissions, and then tells the database to read or write only what's needed. This is called the backend server — think of it as the database's bodyguard.

blocks.alt: Student A sends a request to the backend server and receives a response. The backend server and database are inside one PC, with a curved arrow from the server to the database. Student B's browser is also shown.
blocks.caption: In this example, the backend server and database run on the same PC. The arrows show Student A's request, the database operation, and the response.

blocks.text: On the flip side, the Next.js server that answers with the pages users actually see is called the frontend server. So far, the Ohana Link project has only ever been a frontend server.

Bottom line: running a database means running an always-on computer, the database program on top of it, and a backend server guarding the front door — all three, as a package. When you commission database work, that whole package is what you're signing off on.

steps.title: Use Supabase instead of building it all yourself

blocks.text: Building that whole stack by hand takes a long time and a pile of new concepts. So in this course we use Supabase, which provides all of the following in the cloud, for free:
Database hosting
A backend server
Security, monitoring, and analytics
Authentication — sign-up and log-in features
Unless your user count explodes, you can build your service without worrying about cost, and because Supabase is so popular there are plenty of examples and guides to lean on.

rows: A program that stores large amounts of data in a structured, searchable way
The program that manages the data — colloquially lumped in with “the database”
The go-between that receives user requests, checks permissions, and talks to the database
The server (our Next.js app) that responds with the pages users see
A cloud service that hosts the database, backend, security, and auth for you

blocks.text: Over the rest of this chapter we will:
Create a Supabase project and have the AI connect its SDK to our app
Organize the database into tables — a links table and a folders table
Connect the two tables with a foreign key
Direct the AI to wire every feature of the Ohana Link project to the database

lessons.title: How Databases Work
lessons.objective: Understand tables, primary keys, and foreign keys — well enough to review next lesson's table design and spot when it's been done wrong.

intro.text: In this lesson we look at how the database Supabase gives you actually operates on the inside. Get comfortable with the chain of ideas — tables, then primary keys, then foreign keys — and reviewing the tables the AI creates in the next lesson will feel much easier.

blocks.text: A database keeps data in the form of tables, just like Excel or Google Sheets. Take student records as an example: one table with four columns — student ID, name, year, and grade — can represent them all.
Column: one attribute the data has
Row: one individual piece of data (a record)

steps.title: The primary key: the column that represents each row

blocks.text: A column that holds values that can never repeat — like the student ID — is the one you should designate as the primary key. Once a column is the primary key, the database automatically guarantees two things:
If the same value comes in again it's automatically rejected → duplicate data can't pile up
Every record can be uniquely identified

No column with naturally unique values? Create a new id column and switch on AUTO INCREMENT. Each new row is automatically numbered 1, 2, 3, … in the order it arrives, so the column naturally does the job of a primary key.

When the same information repeats across many rows, you waste storage and performance suffers. If the student table also carried each student's school name and school address, that school info would be duplicated for every student attending the same school.
In cases like this, you split the table:
student table: information unique to each student
school table: school information — one row per school

steps.title: Connecting tables with a foreign key

blocks.text: Split the tables and a new problem appears: you can no longer tell which school a student belongs to. So you add a column like school_id to the student table and have it reference the `id` of the `school` table. A connecting column like this is called a foreign key.

blocks.alt: Student and School tables with school_id and id highlighted. Arrows connect each student’s school_id to the matching School id. Jordan, Maya, and Olivia reference school 0, Ethan references school 1, and Noah references school 2.
blocks.caption: Jordan, Maya, and Olivia share school_id 0. They all reference Pacific University. A foreign key value can repeat in the Student table.

blocks.text: A foreign key can also carry policies that make it follow along when the thing it references changes:
If a school row's id changes → school_id updates automatically
If a school row is deleted → the matching school_id values are deleted too (or emptied out)

The tables exist, but a link still needs a way to identify its folder. This prompt adds `folder_id` to the `link` table. It points to an existing `id` in the `folder` table.

lessons.title: Troubleshooting Database Errors
lessons.objective: When an error appears after database integration, pinpoint the cause yourself — so you hand the AI a precise diagnosis instead of blindly dumping the problem on it.

blocks.text: If things suddenly stop working after integration, the very first thing to check is whether your Supabase project is still running.
“The Supabase free tier automatically pauses a project after one week with no database requests. (As of May 2026.)”
blocks.title: Another way to think about it

blocks.text: Open the project dashboard: if you see the message The project ... is currently paused, the project has been suspended.

blocks.alt: A paused Supabase project and its Resume project control.
blocks.caption: A paused Supabase project and its Resume project control.

blocks.text: A paused free-tier project. Click Resume project to bring it back.
Just click the Resume project button on screen to spin it back up. Restarting takes about 5–15 minutes on average.

If the project is up but a specific feature still fails, the next step is to examine the network requests between your browser and the Supabase backend server. This is a check you run yourself — it's how you turn “it's broken” into a work order the AI can act on.
